questions.question: What are the core concepts in Spring Batch — Job, Step, Chunk, and Tasklet — and how do they relate to each other?
questions.title: Spring Batch Core Concepts: Job, Step, Chunk, and Tasklet
questions.direct_answer: A Job is the top-level container representing an entire batch process, composed of one or more Steps executed in sequence or conditionally. Each Step can follow either a chunk-oriented model (read-process-write in fixed-size chunks) or a Tasklet model (a single custom unit of work). Together, they give you fine-grained control over large-volume data processing with built-in restart and retry support.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Spring Batch's execution model before writing any code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Tasklet with Chunk — candidates often think Tasklet is just a simpler Step, not realizing they are mutually exclusive execution strategies within a Step
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention JobRepository, JobExecution, and StepExecution as the persistence layer that enables restartability — most candidates skip this

sections.title: Spring Batch's Chunk Model Is Not Just 'Process Records in Groups' — It's a Specific Transaction Boundary Design
sections.content:
Spring Batch was designed for one problem: processing millions of records reliably, with the ability to recover from failures without reprocessing everything. The domain model was designed around that constraint.

A **Job** is the top-level unit of work — 'process today's orders', 'generate monthly invoices'. A Job is composed of **Steps**, each of which does one discrete piece of the work. Each Step chooses one of two mutually exclusive execution strategies.

**Chunk-oriented processing** is the standard model: read N items → process each → write all N in a single transaction. The chunk size is the commit interval — every N items, the transaction commits and progress is persisted. If the job fails at item 7001 with chunk size 100, it restarts at item 7001 (the last committed chunk boundary), not at item 1.

**Tasklet** is for everything that isn't record-by-record processing: downloading a file, sending an email, truncating a staging table, calling an external API once. A Tasklet is a `RepeatStatus.FINISHED` or `RepeatStatus.CONTINUABLE` return from a single `execute()` method. **Chunk and Tasklet are mutually exclusive** — a step is either chunk-oriented or tasklet-based. This is the `common_mistake` the interviewer is checking: candidates who think Tasklet is a simplified chunk step.

Spring Batch persists execution state in a **JobRepository** — backed by a relational database. Every Job, Step, and chunk execution is recorded. This metadata enables restartability, auditing, and multi-instance coordination.

The distinction between Chunk and Tasklet is **the most common mistake** this question tests. Candidates often describe Tasklet as a 'simpler chunk step' — it isn't. They are mutually exclusive execution strategies. You cannot have both a chunk-oriented reader/writer AND a Tasklet on the same Step. Choose one: chunk model for iterating over records, Tasklet model for discrete one-time operations.

sections.title: The Transaction Boundary in Chunk Processing — Why Write Phase Failure Is Different From Read Failure
sections.content:
Understanding the chunk transaction boundary explains most Spring Batch debugging. Each chunk runs inside a single transaction that spans the entire read-process-write cycle for those N items.

The read phase calls `ItemReader.read()` repeatedly until the chunk size is reached or `null` is returned (data exhausted). Read failures are handled per-item and can be configured with retry and skip policies. **But read failures don't affect the transaction** — they happen before the transaction boundary or during item reading within the chunk.

The **write phase is different.** The entire chunk's list of processed items is passed to `ItemWriter.write(Chunk<O> items)` in one call. If the write fails, the entire chunk transaction rolls back — all N items that were successfully read and processed are discarded and must be reprocessed. This is the architectural reason Spring Batch recommends keeping ItemWriter idempotent.

The commit interval is the key tuning parameter. Too small (chunk size 1) means one transaction per item — safe but slow due to commit overhead. Too large (chunk size 10,000) means a failure partway through requires reprocessing thousands of items. For most workloads, 100-500 items per chunk balances throughput with restart granularity.

`@StepScope` is essential for readers and writers that depend on job parameters or runtime data. Without it, a singleton reader shared across multiple job executions would maintain state between runs — a subtle bug that only manifests when running multiple jobs concurrently.

sections.title: The JobRepository and Execution Metadata — What Happens Under the Hood at Startup
sections.content:
When a Job is launched, Spring Batch creates a **JobInstance** — the combination of Job name and JobParameters. If this combination has never run before, it's a new instance. If it has run before and failed, the existing instance restarts from the last checkpoint.

Spring Batch creates tables in your database: `BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE`, `BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION`, `BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION_PARAMS`, `BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION`. The schema ships with Spring Batch — `schema-h2.sql`, `schema-mysql.sql`, etc. For tests, an in-memory H2 database with the schema is convenient. **Never use the in-memory `MapJobRepositoryFactoryBean` in production** — it can't persist state across restarts.

The **JobExecution** records the state of a single run attempt: start time, end time, exit status (`COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `STOPPED`). If a Job runs twice with the same parameters and the first run completed successfully, Spring Batch throws a `JobInstanceAlreadyCompleteException` on the second launch — protecting against accidental re-runs. To force a new run for the same business parameters, use `RunIdIncrementer` to add a technical `run.id` parameter.

In production, run only one instance of a given Job with given parameters at a time. Spring Batch doesn't prevent concurrent execution by default — configure your scheduler to prevent overlap or use Spring Batch's `@JobScope` and `JobExecutionDecider` for execution flow control.

The **interview insight** the `to_stand_out` field targets: most candidates describe Spring Batch as 'processes records in batches' and stop there. The JobRepository is the feature that actually differentiates Spring Batch from writing a simple for-loop with a batch insert. Without JobRepository persistence, you get no automatic restart, no audit trail, no idempotency protection, and no visibility into what failed. It's the metadata model that makes Spring Batch suitable for production financial and operational batch processing. Mentioning this demonstrates you've actually used it in production rather than just read about it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Job → Steps → Chunk/Tasklet is the hierarchy** — a `Job` is a complete batch process; a `Step` is one phase (read, process, write or a single task); `Chunk` and `Tasklet` are the two execution models for a step.
- **`JobRepository` persists every execution — it is not optional** — Spring Batch stores `JobInstance`, `JobExecution`, and `StepExecution` in the database; without it, restart, skip, and retry do not work.
- **Chunk processing is transactional per chunk, not per record** — a chunk of 100 items is read, processed, and written inside one transaction; a write failure rolls back only that chunk's 100 items.
- **Tasklet is for single operations that are not read-process-write** — file cleanup, API calls, DDL operations, or sending a completion notification; implement `Tasklet` and return `RepeatStatus.FINISHED`.
- **`JobInstance` = Job + JobParameters; `JobExecution` = one run attempt** — re-running a failed job with the same parameters creates a new `JobExecution` for the existing `JobInstance`, not a new instance.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Batch structures batch processing around a clear hierarchy: Job → Step → Chunk or Tasklet. Every level has a well-defined responsibility and is persisted to the `JobRepository`.

**The hierarchy**
- `Job`: the overall batch process — 'import monthly invoices'; composed of one or more Steps in sequence or conditionally
- `Step`: one phase of the job — 'read from CSV', 'validate records', 'write to database'; each step has its own execution status and can be restarted independently
- `Chunk`: the read-process-write model for a step; reads N items, processes each, writes the batch — all inside one transaction
- `Tasklet`: a single operation for a step — not a read-process-write loop; `execute()` returns `RepeatStatus.FINISHED` or `RepeatStatus.CONTINUABLE`

**`JobRepository` — the persistence layer**
- Stores `JobInstance` (logical job run), `JobExecution` (physical attempt), `StepExecution` (per-step state)
- Enables: restart from the last successful checkpoint; skip counting; retry tracking; execution history
- Spring Boot auto-configures `JobRepository` using the application's `DataSource`

**Chunk transaction model**
- Chunk size 100: reads 100 records, processes each, writes all 100 in one transaction
- A write failure rolls back only that chunk — already committed chunks are not re-processed on restart
- Larger chunks = fewer transactions = better throughput; smaller chunks = finer-grained checkpointing
